strengths: The paper identifies a genuine and important gap in typographic-attack research: prior evaluations focus on object recognition and implicitly reward text-ignoring behavior, which is misaligned with real-world requirements for joint object+text reasoning. The motivation is compelling and clearly articulated.

The Read-or-Ignore VQA (RIO-VQA) formulation via orthogonal axes (Object/Text question type × Clean/Attacked condition) is conceptually clean and enables controlled counterfactual evaluation. The same-scene counterfactual design (varying only question type and attack presence/word) is a principled way to isolate selective text-use ability from confounding factors.

RIO-Bench construction is carefully engineered: using TextVQA + Open Images dual annotations enables paired object/text questions on the same images; hierarchical negative sampling avoids trivial/ambiguous choices; attacks are designed to avoid occluding true text; distance- and similarity-based difficulty levels are sensible.

The evaluation is broad: six LVLMs of varying scale/architecture, three defense classes (CoT, IT-RT, RIO-RT), three attack levels for object-VQA and two for text-VQA, plus LoRA placement ablation, attention visualization, data-size ablation, and generalization to Typo-D and text-centric VQA benchmarks.

The R-CLIP-M metric jointly rewards alignment with ground-truth classes and penalizes attack-word similarity, which is a reasonable way to encode both correctness and robustness in open-ended object-VQA.

Empirical findings are informative: RIO-RT attains strong object robustness without sacrificing text reading (and even improves text-attack robustness), whereas IT-RT gains robustness by effectively discarding reading ability; the LoRA ablation suggesting language-side reasoning drives selective text use is interesting and contrasts with prior vision-centric defenses.
The paper is clearly written and the supplementary material provides detailed construction, metrics, and prompts, aiding reproducibility.
weaknesses: The benchmark is built on a single source (TextVQA + Open Images), which limits scene diversity and may bias the constructed object/text questions to domain-specific characteristics (e.g., object classes tied to natural scenes). The paper acknowledges this but does not validate cross-source generalization of the benchmark itself.

Some supplementary figure examples show the text question 'what kind of beer is this?' repeatedly attached to unrelated scenes (monitor, watch, whiteboard), which is inconsistent and suggests either a figure-preparation error or a deeper alignment bug in question construction. As presented, this is a substantive reproducibility/quality concern that must be resolved.

The proposed RIO-RT 'defense' is essentially supervised fine-tuning on a balanced mixture of the author-constructed Obj-Attack and Text-Attack splits. Its novelty is incremental—the conceptual contribution is the training split enabled by the benchmark—and the paper does not compare against other plausible data-mixture or curriculum strategies, nor against additional inference-time prompting baselines beyond CoT.

Attack generation quality is not validated: object attack words come from CLIP-based negatives and text-attack distractors from Llama-3 without human verification of plausibility, difficulty, or whether a human could solve Text-Attack cases. The 'hard' bucket is empirically defined by proximity, but its validity as a perceptual difficulty axis is asserted rather than demonstrated.

The R-CLIP-M metric is newly introduced and its discriminative validity is not established (e.g., no correlation study with human judgments, no analysis of how top-k choice affects rankings). Slight changes in k or prompt templates could shift results.

In several models (e.g., LLaVA-1.5-7B, Qwen2.5, Qwen3), IT-RT matches or exceeds RIO-RT on object-VQA robustness and by large margins on some subsets, weakening the claim that balanced read/ignore exposure is critical for object-side robustness; the differentiator is largely Text-VQA preservation. The narrative could more carefully disentangle which capability each strategy buys.

No evaluation on frontier closed-source LVLMs (GPT-4V/4o, Gemini, Claude), which would strengthen claims about generality across 'strong LVLMs'. The set of evaluated models, while diverse, is biased toward open-weight models.

The layout/attack overlay approach is purely digital and simplistic; no physical or scene-coherent insertion (as in SceneTAP), which limits claims about practical transferability despite the paper motivating real-world deployment scenarios.

Statement 'first attempt of its kind' for open-ended text-VQA typographic attacks is asserted without fully surveying related textual VQA attack work; the actual attack design (LLM-generated contradictory phrases) is straightforward and could benefit from stronger justification of why this is non-trivial.

strengths: Addresses an important gap: prior typographic-attack evaluations focus on object recognition and can incentivize text suppression, while real applications require joint object-text reasoning.
Formalizes a useful four-way taxonomy (object/text questions x clean/attacked images) and operationalizes it with same-scene counterfactuals in RIO-Bench.
Benchmark construction is fairly large-scale, with dual annotations from TextVQA and Open Images, multiple attack levels, MC/OE formats, and explicit train/val splits.
Evaluates a broad set of recent LVLMs and defenses, providing a useful empirical snapshot of the robustness-versus-reading trade-off.
The finding that one-sided ignore-text training (IT-RT) sharply degrades text reading, while balanced training (RIO-RT) better preserves it, supports the paper's central motivation.
Ablations on LoRA placement and attention visualizations offer some insight into where selective behavior may arise, suggesting a language-side reasoning effect.
Appendix includes cross-dataset generalization and data-size analyses, which strengthen the empirical study beyond the main paper.
The paper is generally well organized and clearly written, making the proposed task and benchmark easy to follow.
weaknesses: No human validation or human baseline is provided for RIO-Bench. For a benchmark paper, it is critical to verify that object-centric questions are unambiguous, text-attack questions remain answerable, and the injected text is actually misleading to humans. The paper asserts fairness but provides no human study or inter-annotator agreement.

The 'selective text use' task may be partially solvable by a shallow question-type shortcut: object questions versus text questions explicitly cue whether text should be used. The benchmark does not test within-question-type selective reading/ignoring based on image context, which weakens the claimed context-aware selective behavior.

Object-centric questions are generated automatically with CLIP-similarity label selection and no human verification. This can introduce label noise, ambiguity, and class-selection artifacts; for open-ended evaluation, using pruned Open Images labels as gold answers may penalize correct outputs not present in the annotation set.

Object-centric attacks are simplistic random text overlays rather than scene-coherent or physically plausible attacks. This may make the benchmark easier and less realistic than real-world typographic attacks, and the paper does not analyze attack realism or human detectability.

The proposed R-CLIP-M metric is not clearly justified and may be problematic: it uses text-text CLIP top-5 retrieval over all classes and subtracts attack-word retrieval. This can give credit for semantically related but incorrect predictions, is unbounded, and is reported as 'Acc.' in tables, which is misleading.

Text-attack generation uses an LLM to create contradictory words, but there is limited validation that the generated distractors are plausible, semantically misleading, and not trivially ignorable. Distance-based difficulty only controls spatial proximity, not semantic confusability.

The proposed RIO-RT defense is essentially supervised fine-tuning on the benchmark's own training data with a balanced attack mixture. It is not a new defense algorithm, and the comparison against IT-RT is somewhat expected because IT-RT is explicitly one-sided. Missing baselines include fine-tuning on clean data only, clean+attack mixtures, and standard augmentation/regularization defenses.

Main-paper evaluation is largely in-domain, training and testing on RIO-Bench splits. Cross-dataset generalization is relegated to the appendix, and some results show RIO-RT still degrades text reading (e.g., SmolVLM-2B) or improves it suspiciously (e.g., Llama-3.2-11B on ChartQA), raising questions about the robustness of the conclusions.

The Text-Clean branch discards most TextVQA QA pairs by keeping only the smallest-index QA per image. This reduces linguistic diversity, may introduce arbitrary selection artifacts, and the effect of this choice is not analyzed.

The claim that 'existing defenses fail' is supported by a narrow set of defenses: only CoT for LVLMs plus a reimplemented ignore-text training baseline. Other defenses are either not applicable to modern LVLMs or not compared directly.
No error bars or multiple seeds are reported for training-based comparisons, so the reported gains may not be statistically reliable.

Some claims, such as 'first structural foundation for training-based defenses' and 'genuinely new capability', are stronger than the evidence supports given the incremental nature of the defense and the lack of human validation.

strengths: Introduces a well-motivated unified task, RIO-VQA, that jointly evaluates typographic robustness and text-reading ability, addressing a real gap in LVLM evaluation.
RIO-Bench is carefully constructed using same-scene counterfactuals from TextVQA and Open Images dual annotations, with controlled attack levels and balanced question types.
Comprehensive experiments across six LVLMs and multiple defenses show that current models and text-ignoring defenses fail to balance robustness and reading, substantiating the paper's central claim.

The proposed RIO-RT defense demonstrably improves selective text use, maintaining text-reading performance while boosting object-attack robustness, and generalizes to external Typo-D and text-VQA benchmarks.
Additional analyses (LoRA placement, attention visualization, data-size ablation) provide useful insight into where and how selective text-use behavior is learned.
The paper is clear, well-organized, and provides sufficient implementation and dataset-construction details for reproducibility.
weaknesses: RIO-Bench is instantiated only on TextVQA/Open Images scene text; despite claims of adaptability, the current benchmark does not cover broader domains such as documents, charts, or physically realistic scene-coherent attacks, limiting external validity.

Some evaluation choices are ad hoc, especially the R-CLIP-M metric that combines CLIP-M@5 with an attack-word penalty; this may conflate correctness and robustness and could be sensitive to top-k and prompt/template choices.

The selective text-use capability is trained with explicit question-type supervision, so it remains unclear whether models learn genuine context-aware reading/ignoring or a question-type shortcut; deeper probing would strengthen the claim.

Comparisons to existing defenses are limited: CoT is reproduced, and other CLIP-era defenses are adapted into IT-RT/RIO-RT, but direct LVLM-specific defenses may be missing; the IT-RT baseline's odd generalization behavior also complicates interpretation.

Claims about language-component governance and attention behavior rely on LoRA experiments and qualitative attention maps from limited models; statistical significance and variance across training runs are not reported.

The proposed RIO-RT is primarily supervised fine-tuning on attacked data from the same benchmark, so its novelty as a defense mechanism is moderate and its robustness to unseen attack styles remains to be fully established.

strengths: The paper identifies a real and well-motivated gap: typographic-attack robustness and scene-text reading are usually evaluated separately, while real-world LVLM use often requires deciding when to read and when to ignore in-image text.

The proposed RIO-VQA task and same-scene counterfactual design are conceptually clean: crossing question intent with clean/attack conditions enables controlled comparisons under a fixed underlying scene, reducing common confounds from using different datasets for reading and robustness.

The benchmark construction is substantial: TextVQA, Open Images labels, hierarchical negative sampling, controlled overlay attacks, SceneTAP-based scene-coherent insertions, OCR-aware placement, and a human audit all support the benchmark's validity and reusability.

The experimental evaluation is broad: multiple LVLM families and scales, modern/frontier models, several defense baselines, attack difficulty levels, LoRA placement ablation, attention visualization, and external transfer to TypoD and text-heavy VQA datasets.

The central empirical finding is useful and clearly supported: object-centric robustness training can improve attack performance by reducing text sensitivity, harming text-reading performance, whereas balanced read-or-ignore training can improve both on RIO-Bench.
The paper is largely reproducible: prompts, attack construction details, training hyperparameters, metrics, computational cost, and qualitative examples are provided in the appendix.
The RIO-RT baseline, while simple, demonstrates the intended behavior and provides a reference point for future work; the benchmark also supplies explicit training and validation splits.
weaknesses: Automatic benchmark construction may introduce label and answer noise: object ground-truth labels are chosen by CLIP similarity rather than human verification, and text-centric attack words are generated by an LLM. The human audit on 400 samples is reassuring but not comprehensive enough to fully validate the dataset at scale.

The same-scene counterfactual claim is only partially matched: Obj-Attack and Text-Attack use different inserted distractor text, so attack condition is not identical across question intents. This can leave residual confounding when comparing read-versus-ignore behavior across settings.

The proposed R-CLIP-M metric is novel and not thoroughly validated. Subtracting the attack-word retrieval score may conflate whether the model mentions the distractor with whether it actually relies on it, and the choice of K=5 is not justified or ablated.

The RIO-RT defense is trained on the benchmark's own attack distribution, so its strong results may partly reflect in-distribution adaptation. The comparison with IT-RT also confounds data mixture and task objective in ways that make it difficult to isolate why RIO-RT succeeds.

Main results lack error bars or statistical significance tests, and some tables are hard to parse in the supplied manuscript due to formatting and apparent typos (e.g., inconsistent model names, garbled columns, and unclear relative-change annotations).

Attack realism is limited: Overlay-Attack uses randomized digital text, while SceneTAP-Attack is closer to real-world typography but is only used for evaluation and includes safeguards that may weaken the attacks. Physical, handwritten, adaptive, and multi-text attacks are not covered.

The defense comparison is narrow. Many CLIP-based defenses are not adapted, and CoT is only one LVLM-focused baseline; the conclusion that language-side adaptation is key rests on a limited LoRA-placement study across two models.

Clarity and presentation need improvement. The paper is generally organized well, but several figures/tables are difficult to read in the supplied version, and some appendix tables contain obvious typos or inconsistent entries that undermine confidence in the exact numbers.

strengths: The paper addresses a timely and practically important problem: jointly evaluating typographic-attack robustness and scene-text reading in LVLMs, rather than treating them as separate capabilities.

The proposed RIO-VQA taxonomy and same-scene counterfactual design are conceptually appealing. Building on TextVQA plus Open Images annotations to create paired object- and text-centric questions under clean and attacked conditions is a reasonable benchmark construction strategy.

The benchmark is large in scale (roughly 242K training and 35K evaluation instances according to the appendix), includes controlled overlay attacks and scene-coherent generative insertions, and provides a training split for future work.
The paper includes a human audit of 400 samples with reported inter-annotator agreement, which is a positive step toward benchmark quality validation.
The empirical study covers several recent LVLMs, including open-source and frontier models, with analyses of scaling, attack difficulty, trainable parameter placement, and attention maps.

The proposed RIO-RT baseline illustrates that balanced exposure to object- and text-centric attacked data can improve robustness while largely preserving text reading, and the paper honestly lists some limitations.
weaknesses: The benchmark construction has unresolved validity concerns. Object-centric QA is generated automatically from CLIP-selected Open Images labels, but there is no large-scale human verification of whether the selected object is truly the intended ground-truth object, whether the generated question is natural, and whether hierarchical negatives are plausible. The 400-sample audit checks answerability and distractor validity, but it does not fully validate the central object-centric QA design.

The same-scene counterfactual claim is somewhat overstated. The four subsets vary not only question intent and text condition but also QA format, answer space, evaluation metric, and question-generation method. This makes direct comparisons across settings harder than the paper acknowledges, and it weakens the claim that the benchmark isolates read-or-ignore behavior.

The attack design is limited. Overlay attacks use randomized placement outside OCR regions, which may be unrealistic and often weak; text-centric attacks rely on LLM-generated contradictory phrases whose semantic plausibility is not extensively validated; near-placement attacks are discarded, potentially reducing the strength and realism of the benchmark. SceneTAP-Attack preserves OCR regions, which is good for safety but may also make the attack less realistic.

The R-CLIP-M metric is non-standard and potentially problematic. It subtracts an attack-word retrieval score from CLIP-M and is not bounded below, so scores can become negative and are difficult to interpret as accuracy. The metric conflates retrieval errors with robustness to distractor text, and it is not rigorously justified or compared with alternative evaluation protocols.

The defense evaluation is confounded by fine-tuning effects. RIO-RT and IT-RT are trained on RIO-Bench training subsets, but there is no clean-only SFT control, random-text control, or other control showing that improvements are specifically due to read-or-ignore learning rather than generic task-format adaptation and LoRA fine-tuning. This weakens the central claim that object-centric defenses suppress text sensitivity and that RIO-RT induces the desired selective behavior.

The paper’s main finding is somewhat exaggerated. IT-RT is explicitly trained on object-centric attacked data only, so its degradation on text-centric questions is largely expected by construction. A balanced data mixture (RIO-RT) already mitigates the trade-off, suggesting that the issue is data coverage and training objective rather than a fundamental misalignment of existing robustness work.

Experimental presentation and reproducibility are not convincing in the supplied manuscript. Tables 3 and 7 are difficult to parse and contain apparently inconsistent or implausible entries, e.g., IT-RT OV_e = 47.9 while OV_m/OV_h are around 98, and repeated identical values across many Table 7 cells. There are no confidence intervals, multiple seeds, or detailed statistical tests, and the claimed consistency across six LVLMs is not always supported by the reported numbers.

The task definition does not fully match the claimed “decide from context” capability. RIO-Bench explicitly provides the question intent (object vs. text) in the prompt, so it evaluates conditional reading/ignoring given a stated intent rather than autonomous context-aware read-or-ignore decision making. Real-world scenes often require inferring whether text should be read or ignored, which is a harder and more central challenge.

Missing baselines and analyses: there is no human upper bound, no OCR-only or vision-only reference, no evaluation of whether models actually use the distractor versus the relevant scene text in ambiguous cases, and no comparison with additional defense families beyond CoT and the paper’s own SFT variants. Out-of-benchmark generalization is claimed but not convincingly demonstrated due to the confusing table presentation.

strengths: The paper identifies a real blind spot in typographic-attack evaluation: object-centric robustness can be achieved by suppressing text sensitivity, which is undesirable when models also need to read scene text.
It formulates RIO-VQA, a useful and practically motivated task requiring context-dependent read-or-ignore behavior rather than unconditional text ignoring.
RIO-Bench is carefully designed as a same-scene counterfactual benchmark built on TextVQA/Open Images, with matched object/text and clean/attack subsets that reduce scene-level confounds.

The benchmark construction is relatively thorough: hierarchical negative sampling, OCR-aware overlay placement, two attack settings (controlled overlays and scene-coherent SceneTAP), and a human audit with high agreement.

The experimental study is broad, covering multiple LVLMs, representative defenses, attack difficulty levels, LoRA placement, and attention visualization, and it convincingly exposes the robustness-vs-text-reading trade-off.

The proposed RIO-RT baseline is simple, architecture-agnostic, and shows that balanced training on object- and text-centric attacked data can improve robustness while largely preserving scene-text understanding.
The paper includes generalization checks to SceneTAP attacks and external text-centric VQA benchmarks, and the appendix provides substantial reproducibility detail for data construction and training.
As a dataset/benchmark contribution, RIO-Bench is likely to be useful for future work on typographic robustness in LVLMs, especially because it exposes behavior that object-centric protocols miss.
weaknesses: The benchmark is built solely on TextVQA/Open Images, which limits scene diversity, text distribution, and applicability to broader real-world typographic attacks, including physical or more naturalistic settings.

The object-centric questions are synthetically generated from Open Images labels, so they may differ in style and difficulty from natural object-VQA questions; although human audit is reassuring, automated generation can still introduce biases.

Attack difficulty is defined heuristically by semantic or spatial proximity, and the overlay attacks are relatively controlled; the extent to which these reflect real typographic threat models remains uncertain.
R-CLIP-M is a custom metric that can be negative and depends on CLIP embeddings, candidate class vocabulary, and the choice of K; it would benefit from stronger validation and sensitivity analysis.

The RIO-RT training study is limited to a single SFT recipe and Overlay-Attack training data, and improvements are not uniformly large across models; broader training objectives and out-of-distribution robustness remain open.
Comparison to prior defenses is somewhat limited: many CLIP-specific defenses are not directly adapted, and the main prior LVLM defense compared is CoT prompting.
Some claims, such as a 'fundamental misalignment,' are stronger than what a single benchmark may fully establish, even if the evidence is suggestive.

The results tables in the supplied manuscript appear partially garbled or inconsistent in model names/numbers, making exact verification difficult; this should be carefully corrected for camera-ready presentation.
The paper does not explicitly state public release, licensing, or maintenance plans for the benchmark/code, which matters for a dataset/benchmark contribution.
